prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

RUN AWAY from this sub- scriber for the second time are TWO NEGROES, viz. SMART, an outlandish dark fellow with his country marks on his temples and bearing the remarkable brand of my name on his left breast, last seen wearing an old ragged negro cloth shirt and breeches made of fearnought; also DIDO, a likely young wench of a yellow cast, born in cherrytime in this parish, wearing a mixed coloured coat with a bundle of clothes, mostly blue, under her one good arm. Both speak tolerable plain English and may insist on being called Cuffee and Khasa respect- ively. Whoever shall deliver the said goods to the gaoler in Baton Rouge, or to the Sugar House in the parish, shall receive all reasonable charges plus a genteel reward besides what the law allows. In the mean time all persons are strictly forbid harbouring them, on pain of being prosecuted to the utmost rigour of the law. Ten guineas will be paid to anyone who can give intelligence of their being harboured, employed, or enter- tained by a white person upon his sentence; five on conviction of a black. All Masters of vessels are warned against carrying them out of state, as they may claim to be free. If any of the above Negroes return of their own accord, they may still be for- given by ELIZABETH YOUNG.

outputs.L2:
For the second time, two enslaved people have escaped from the undersigned. The first, SMART, is a dark-skinned African-born man with traditional markings on his temples and the advertiser’s name conspicuously branded on his left breast. When last observed, he had on a worn, torn shirt made of “negro cloth” and fearnought breeches. The second, DIDO, is a healthy-looking young woman with a yellow complexion. She was born during cherry season in this parish. She wore a multicoloured coat and carried beneath her only sound arm a bundle containing clothes, chiefly blue.

Both speak fairly clear English. SMART may call himself Cuffee, while DIDO may use the name Khasa. Anyone who takes them to the Baton Rouge jailer or to the parish Sugar House will be reimbursed for all reasonable expenses and given a generous reward in addition to the amount provided by law.

No one is to shelter them; offenders will be prosecuted with the full severity of the law. Ten guineas will be awarded for information proving that a white person has housed, employed, or otherwise accommodated them, provided that person is sentenced. Five guineas will be paid upon the conviction of a Black person for the same offense.

Shipmasters are cautioned not to transport either person out of the state, since they may represent themselves as free. If SMART or DIDO returns voluntarily, forgiveness may still be granted by  
**ELIZABETH YOUNG.**

outputs.L4:
Elizabeth Young’s notice announces the escape of two enslaved people, Smart and Dido, and calls for their capture and return. To make them easier to identify, the notice supplies physical descriptions, notes any aliases by which they might be known, and describes the clothing they wore when they left. It also offers monetary rewards, both for returning Smart and Dido and for providing information about people who may have helped them escape. These details effectively invite readers to participate in a broad system of surveillance intended to restrict the fugitives’ movement and prevent them from establishing new lives.

The notice also warns that anyone who shelters, employs, conceals, or transports Smart and Dido may be prosecuted. At the same time, it offers conditional forgiveness to those willing to disclose information or withdraw their assistance. This combination of threats and incentives was designed to isolate escaped enslaved people from potential allies. By rewarding capture, encouraging informants, and invoking the power of the law, Young’s notice demonstrates how slavery was maintained not only through direct physical control but also through financial pressure, public surveillance, and legal coercion. Although the document presents Smart and Dido as property to be recovered, their escape also reveals their resistance to enslavement and their effort to claim freedom for themselves.
outputs.L5:
## Run Away, Two

“Run away,” she whispered.

The words hung between the two of them like a door left open.

Outside, dawn crept over the sleeping town. They had no map, little money, and no idea what waited beyond the hills. But staying meant accepting a life chosen by others.

He reached for her hand. “Together?”

She smiled.

And so, while the streets were still quiet, the two began to run—not away from life, but toward one they could finally call their own.

> **RUN AWAY**  
> From the Plantation of the Subscriber, near the German Coast, on the Night of the 14th Instant, two Negroes; viz. a Man named **SMART**, about five Feet seven Inches high, stout made, of a dark Complexion, and speaks some French and English; had on when he went away an oznabrig Shirt and coarse Trowsers. Also a Woman named **DIDO**, middle-sized, marked with the Small-Pox, speaks chiefly French, and carried with her a blue Petticoat and checked Handkerchief.  
>

Masters of Vessels, Ferrymen, and others are hereby cautioned against harbouring or carrying them off.  
>   
> **ELIZABETH YOUNG.**  
> Louisiana, Sept. 20, 1798.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a period-style runaway slave notice describing two escapees, their appearance, clothing, alternate names, rewards for capture, and penalties for anyone harbouring them. Format it like imperfect OCR from an old newspaper.

*Fictional archival pastiche; the language reflects the brutality of slavery-era notices.*

---

**RAN AWAY,**

From the subscriber, living near James-River, on the night  
of the 14th inst. two enslaved persons, viz.

**ISAAC**, sometimes calling himself **ISAAC FREEMAN**, or  
**JOHN HILL**; about 27 years of age, five feet eight or nine  
inches high, of a spare make, dark complexion, with a small  
scar over the left eye. Had on when he went away, a brown  
homespun coat much worn at the elbows, oznabrig trowsers, a  
striped waistcoat, and an old felt hat. He reads a little, and  
may produce a forged pass.

Also, **HANNAH**, who is known in some places by the name of  
**ANN CARTER**; about 23 years old, middle stature, strong made,  
with a round face and a mark of a burn upon her right hand.  
She took with her a blue linsey gown, a checked apron, a red  
woollen shawl, and sundry other cloaths not recollected. She  
speaks readily, and may say that she is hired out, or travelling  
to join free relations.

It is supposed they will attempt to reach some northern port,  
and may travel as man and wife. All masters of vessels, stage  
drivers, tavern-keepers, and others, are cautioned against  
carrying or concealing them.

**TWENTY DOLLARS REWARD** will be paid for either, if secured  
in any gaol within this State, or **FIFTY DOLLARS** for both if  
delivered to the subscriber; and a further reasonable allowance  
for expences, if taken beyond the State.

Any person harbouring, employing, or assisting the said run-  
aways will be prosecuted to the utmost rigour of the law, and  
made liable to all fines & penalties thereunto belonging.

                             **THOMAS W———.**  
Henrico County, June 18, 1817.                  [3—tf]

N. B. The above reward will not be paid without satisfactory  
proof of apprehension. Printers in the neighbouring States are  
requested to insert this advertisernent three times, and forward  
their accounts.
